narr: In this section, we're going to explore the fascinating world of linear algebra, focusing on weeks 5 through 7. We'll dive into questions, formulas, and solutions that reveal the beautiful structure of linear systems.
Both pictures are the same equation Ax = b: rows are intersections (equations), columns are linear combinations (vectors).

data.heading: Three possible outcomes
bullets: One solution—independent constraints.
Infinitely many solutions: x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4—the second equation is twice the first, the lines coincide.
No solutions: x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 5—the left sides are proportional, the right sides are not, the lines are parallel.

narr: When solving linear systems, we encounter three possible outcomes. First, there might be exactly one solution, which happens when our constraints are independent.
Second, we might have infinitely many solutions, like when we have equations that are essentially the same, just scaled versions of each other.
Third, there might be no solution at all, which occurs when our constraints contradict each other.

data.heading: Elimination reveals outcome
data.tex: [00 \dots 0|0] \rightarrow 0 = 0 \text{— infinitely many solutions}; [00 \dots 0|c], c \neq 0 \rightarrow 0 = c \text{— no solutions}

parts.note: All zeros in the coefficient matrix with zero on the right
All zeros in the coefficient matrix with non-zero on the right

narr: Gaussian elimination helps us reveal these outcomes. When we end up with all zeros in the coefficient matrix and zero on the right side, we get 0 = 0, which is always true, indicating infinitely many solutions.
But if we have all zeros in the coefficient matrix but a non-zero constant on the right, we get 0 = c, which is a contradiction, meaning no solutions exist.

data.heading: Pivot, multiplier, and forward elimination
bullets: λ_{ij} = \frac{a_{ij}}{a_{jj}}
Operation: R_i ← R_i - λ_{ij} · R_j
To eliminate element a_{ij} below a nonzero pivot a_{jj}, subtract row j multiplied by λ_{ij} from row i.

narr: Let's talk about the key components of elimination: pivots, multipliers, and forward elimination.
The multiplier λ_{ij} is calculated as the ratio of the element we want to eliminate to the pivot element.
The actual elimination operation subtracts the pivot row multiplied by this multiplier from the target row.

data.heading: Running example
steps: Operations: R_2 ← R_2 - 2R_1, R_3 ← R_3 + R_1

narr: Let's walk through a concrete example to see elimination in action.
We start with this augmented matrix. Our first pivot is 2.
The multipliers for eliminating below this pivot are 2 and -1.
Applying the elimination operations gives us this new matrix.
Our second pivot is -8.
The multiplier for eliminating below this pivot is -1.
Applying this final elimination step gives us our triangular system.
The upper triangular matrix U contains our pivots 2, -8, and 1.

data.heading: Back substitution
bullets: Solution: x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
The triangular system is solved from bottom up
The answer is verified by substitution into the original equation

narr: Once we have our triangular system, we solve it using back substitution, working from the bottom up.
The last equation gives us w directly.
The second equation allows us to solve for v once we know w.
The first equation then lets us solve for u.
Our solution vector is [1, 1, 2].
We can verify this by substituting back into the original equation.

parts.note: Original matrix multiplied by solution vector

narr: Here's the verification step. Multiplying our original matrix by the solution vector gives us back the original right-hand side, confirming our solution is correct.

data.heading: Important note
bullets: A row operation is reversible (add 2R_1 back)
Elimination preserves solutions
The operation must be applied to both left and right sides
Otherwise the equations are not equivalent

narr: It's crucial to remember that row operations are reversible, which means elimination preserves solutions.
However, we must apply the same operations to both sides of the equation.
If we don't, the equations won't remain equivalent.

data.heading: Elimination matrices E
bullets: E_{21} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
E_{21} · A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -8 & -2 \\ -2 & 7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
E_{21} · b = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -12 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}
Left multiplication performs a row operation
The right side is transformed by the same matrix
Ax = b becomes (E_{21}A)x = E_{21}b

narr: Each row operation can be represented by an elimination matrix E.
For example, E_{21} performs the operation R_2 ← R_2 - 2R_1.
When we multiply E_{21} by A, we get the transformed matrix.
Similarly, multiplying E_{21} by b transforms the right side.
This shows that left multiplication by E performs the row operation.
The system Ax = b becomes (E_{21}A)x = E_{21}b after the operation.

data.heading: Full elimination process
steps: The rightmost multiplier acts first—order of multiplication matters
Undo step: subtraction is replaced by addition
For E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, the inverse is E^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}

narr: To complete the full elimination process, we multiply by all the elimination matrices in order.
The rightmost multiplier acts first, which is why the order of multiplication matters.
To undo an elimination step, we simply reverse the operation—subtraction becomes addition.
The inverse of an elimination matrix E performs this undo operation.
Multiplying E by its inverse gives us the identity matrix I.

data.heading: Zero pivot: permutation matrices P
bullets: \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & | & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & | & 7 \end{bmatrix} → \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & | & 7 \\ 0 & 2 & | & 4 \end{bmatrix} (row exchange)
Then y = 2, x = 5/3
A zero pivot does not necessarily mean singularity
If there is a nonzero element below, rows are swapped
The swap is performed by a permutation matrix P
P also transforms the right side: PAx = Pb

narr: What happens when we encounter a zero pivot? It doesn't necessarily mean the system is singular.
If there's a nonzero element below the zero pivot, we can swap rows.
This swap is performed by a permutation matrix P.
The permutation matrix also transforms the right side of the equation.
The system becomes PAx = Pb after the permutation.

data.heading: Properties of permutation matrices
steps: One 1 in each row and column, rest zeros
For a single swap P^2 = I
Left multiplication changes equations, not unknowns

narr: Permutation matrices have some interesting properties.
They contain exactly one 1 in each row and column, with zeros elsewhere.
The inverse of a permutation matrix is its transpose.
For a single swap, P squared equals the identity matrix.
When we left-multiply by P, we're changing the equations, not the unknowns.

data.heading: Elimination failures
bullets: Temporary — zero pivot with nonzero element below (swap saves)
Permanent — no available pivot in column (singularity: no solution or infinitely many)

narr: There are two types of elimination failures. Temporary failures occur when we have a zero pivot but a nonzero element below, which we can fix by swapping.
Permanent failures happen when there's no available pivot in a column, indicating singularity—either no solution or infinitely many solutions.

data.heading: Looking ahead: A = LU and PA = LU
bullets: Without row exchanges: A = LU (U — upper triangular, L stores elimination factors)
With exchanges: PA = LU

narr: Looking ahead to future topics, we'll learn about LU decomposition.
Without row exchanges, A can be factored into LU, where U is upper triangular and L stores the elimination factors.
With row exchanges, we have PA = LU, where P is the permutation matrix.

data.heading: Week summary
items: Elimination — zeros below pivots plus back substitution
E — row replacement, P — row swap
LU decomposition (A = LU, PA = LU) is built in week 6

narr: To summarize this week's content:
We've seen how rows represent intersections of equations, while columns represent linear combinations of vectors.
Elimination involves creating zeros below pivots followed by back substitution.
We've introduced elimination matrices E for row replacement and permutation matrices P for row swaps.
Finally, we've previewed LU decomposition, which we'll explore more in week 6.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Row picture and column picture
data.problem: Solve the system \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} and describe both geometric pictures.
steps: Lines 2x - y = 1 and x + y = 5 intersect at (2, 3)

narr: Let's solve our first exercise. We need to solve this 2x2 system and describe both the row and column pictures.
Adding the two equations gives us 3x = 6, so x = 2.
Substituting back, we find y = 5 - 2 = 3.
Geometrically, the lines represented by these equations intersect at the point (2, 3).
In the column picture, we're finding coefficients that combine the column vectors to give the right-hand side vector.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Three outcomes
data.problem: Classify the system \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ c \end{bmatrix} for c = 4 and c = 5.
steps: When c = 4, this is 0 = 0: x + y = 2 remains
data.result: For c = 4: infinitely many solutions; for c = 5: no solution

narr: In this exercise, we classify the system for two different values of c.
Applying elimination, we get a row of [0 0|c - 4].
When c = 4, this becomes 0 = 0, which is always true. We're left with just x + y = 2, giving infinitely many solutions.
When c = 5, we get 0 = 1, which is a contradiction.
So for c = 5, there's no solution.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Find the multiplier
data.problem: Eliminate below the first pivot in the augmented matrix \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & | & 7 \\ 8 & 13 & | & 29 \end{bmatrix} and find both pivots.

narr: For this exercise, we need to find the multiplier and perform elimination.
The multiplier λ_{21} is 8/2 = 4.
Applying the elimination operation R_2 ← R_2 - 4R_1 gives us this new matrix.
The pivots in the resulting matrix are 2 and 1.

data.heading: Problem 4 — Back substitution
data.problem: Solve the system \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}.

narr: Now we practice back substitution on this triangular system.
Starting from the bottom, we find z = 2 directly.
Using this value, we solve for y: 3y + 2 · 2 = 7 gives y = 1.
Finally, we solve for x: 2x + 1 - 2 = 3 gives x = 2.
Our solution is [2, 1, 2], which we verify by substituting back into the original equations.
In this exercise, we perform full elimination on a 3x3 system.
First, we eliminate below the first pivot, getting these two new rows.
Next, we eliminate below the second pivot, resulting in this triangular form.
Now we can solve for z directly: 3z = 10 gives z = 10/3.
Using this value, we solve for y: y - 10/3 = -2 gives y = 4/3.
Finally, we solve for x: x + 4/3 + 10/3 = 6 gives x = 4/3.

data.heading: Problem 6 — Identify elementary matrix
data.problem: Find E that performs R_3 ← R_3 - 4R_1 on a 3 × 3 matrix.
steps: E is identity matrix with -4 in position (3, 1)

narr: For our final exercise, we need to find the elementary matrix that performs a specific row operation.
The matrix E is the identity matrix with -4 in position (3, 1).
When we multiply E by A, row 3 of the result is row 3 minus 4 times row 1, while rows 1 and 2 remain unchanged.
The inverse operation would be addition, so E^{-1} has +4 in position (3, 1).
